concepts.title: What a Mutual Fund Is and Who Runs It
concepts.description: A mutual fund collects money from many small investors and puts it into one asset class such as company shares (equity), loans/bonds (debt), gold or real estate. Each separate product it offers is called a scheme or fund, and one fund house can run many schemes for different needs. Instead of picking securities themselves, investors hire a professional fund manager who selects securities, decides timing, and rebalances the portfolio, in return for a fee. The fund is promoted by a sponsor; trustees are appointed to safeguard investors' interests; and an asset management company (AMC) actually runs the schemes. Registrars & transfer agents (RTA), custodians, distributors, bankers, brokers and depository participants support the operation. SEBI (the market regulator) licenses every one of these for experience and financial soundness. A brand-new scheme is offered to the public through a New Fund Offer (NFO) once the trustees and SEBI approve it; the Key Information Memorandum (KIM) is the short-form offer document handed to investors.
misconceptions: Believing investors directly hold the underlying shares/bonds instead of fund units
Thinking the sponsor makes the day-to-day buy/sell decisions
Assuming mutual fund returns are guaranteed by SEBI or the government

objectives.text: List the three principal constituents of a mutual fund and state each one's role.
Explain why an investor might choose a mutual fund over buying securities directly.

questions.stem: Rekha wants exposure to Indian company shares but has neither the time nor the knowledge to pick individual stocks. She buys units of an equity mutual fund scheme. In legal terms, what does Rekha actually own after this purchase?

options.text: Units of the scheme, which represent her proportional share of the pooled portfolio
The specific shares the fund manager bought, registered directly in her name
options.misconception: Belief that a mutual fund investor directly holds the underlying securities rather than fund units

options.text: A fixed-return deposit receipt issued by the AMC
options.misconception: Confusing a mutual fund scheme with a guaranteed-return bank-style deposit

options.text: A membership share in the sponsor company that promoted the fund
options.misconception: Confusing ownership of fund units with owning equity in the sponsor/AMC

questions.explanation: A mutual fund pools money and issues units; each unit is one share of the fund's overall portfolio (all the securities it holds together). Rekha owns units, not the individual shares themselves and not any stake in the company that set the fund up. The fund is not a fixed-return product, so she does not hold a deposit receipt either.

questions.stem: The chapter names three principal constituents of every mutual fund. Which trio is correct?

options.text: Sponsor, trustees and the asset management company (AMC)
Custodian, distributor and registrar & transfer agent
options.misconception: Mistaking the supporting service providers for the three principal constituents

options.text: SEBI, RBI and AMFI
options.misconception: Confusing the regulators/industry body with the fund's own constituents

options.text: Fund manager, broker and depository participant
options.misconception: Naming operational roles instead of the governing constituents

questions.explanation: The three principal constituents are the sponsor (the promoter who sets the fund up), the trustees (who guard investors' interests), and the AMC (which runs the schemes). Custodians, RTAs, distributors, brokers and depository participants are supporting constituents. SEBI and RBI are regulators and AMFI is the industry body, none of which are the fund's own constituents.

questions.stem: Before a mutual fund can launch a completely new scheme to the public, whose approval must it obtain?

options.text: The trustees and SEBI
Only the sponsor, since it promoted the fund
options.misconception: Assuming the sponsor alone can authorise a new scheme

options.text: The RBI, because all investment products need central-bank clearance
options.misconception: Over-extending RBI's limited role to general scheme approval

options.text: AMFI, as the body that registers all schemes
options.misconception: Treating the industry association AMFI as an approving authority

questions.explanation: A new scheme is floated through a New Fund Offer (NFO — the first sale of units to the public) only after both the trustees and SEBI approve it. RBI is involved only in narrow areas such as foreign-exchange matters, and AMFI is an industry body that recommends best practice, not an approving regulator.

questions.stem: What is the Key Information Memorandum (KIM)?

options.text: An abridged offer document giving investors the essential facts about a scheme
The trust deed that appoints the trustees of the fund
options.misconception: Confusing the investor-facing KIM with the internal trust-formation document

options.text: A monthly account statement of the investor's holdings
options.misconception: Confusing the pre-investment KIM with the post-transaction statement of account

options.text: The custodian's certificate confirming the securities are safely held
options.misconception: Confusing an offer document with a custodial safekeeping record

questions.explanation: The KIM is the short-form version of the full offer document, summarising the essential features of a scheme so an investor can decide. It is not the trust deed, not the periodic account statement, and not any custodial certificate.

concepts.title: Units, NAV and Why Transactions Don't Move the Price
concepts.description: Each investor's stake in a scheme is measured in units, worked out as amount invested divided by price per unit. Net Asset Value (NAV) is the per-unit value of the fund, and it is calculated every business day so investors can value holdings and transact. Units are first sold in the NFO. A key idea: when an investor buys or sells (redeems) units at the correct NAV, the NAV itself does not change, because the money coming in or going out is matched by units being created or cancelled. NAV only moves when the value of the portfolio's securities changes, or if the fund wrongly allots/redeems units at a price different from NAV, which unfairly affects every other investor. The value of any investor's holding equals number of units held times the current NAV.
prerequisites: What a Mutual Fund Is and Who Runs It
misconceptions: Thinking buying or redeeming units at NAV pushes the NAV up or down
Believing NAV changes daily only because of investor inflows/outflows
Assuming a higher NAV means a better or more expensive-to-own fund

objectives.text: Compute units allotted and the value of a holding from the amount invested and the NAV.
Explain why a purchase or redemption transacted at NAV leaves the NAV unchanged.

questions.stem: Manish invests Rs.20,000 in a scheme when its NAV (per-unit price) is Rs.25. How many units is he allotted?

options.text: 800 units
500,000 units
options.misconception: Multiplying amount by NAV instead of dividing

options.text: 25 units
options.misconception: Dividing NAV by amount, i.e. inverting the formula

options.text: 20,000 units
options.misconception: Assuming one rupee buys one unit, ignoring the NAV

questions.explanation: Units = amount invested / NAV. Here 20,000 / 25 = 800 units. Multiplying (20,000 x 25) or inverting the division gives the wrong figures; and the NAV of Rs.25, not Rs.1, is the price of each unit.

questions.stem: A scheme has net assets of Rs.1,00,000 spread over 10,000 units, so NAV is Rs.10. An investor now buys 1,000 fresh units at this NAV of Rs.10. What is the NAV immediately after the purchase?

options.text: Rs.10 — unchanged, because the extra Rs.10,000 of assets is matched by 1,000 extra units
Rs.11, because the new money increases the fund's total assets
options.misconception: Thinking inflows raise NAV even when units are issued at NAV

options.text: Rs.9.09, because the units outstanding rose
options.misconception: Thinking new units dilute NAV even when matched by equal assets

options.text: Rs.10,000, confusing the NAV with the amount the investor brought in
options.misconception: Confusing per-unit NAV with the total transaction value

questions.explanation: New assets = 1,000 x Rs.10 = Rs.10,000, so assets become Rs.1,10,000 and units become 11,000. NAV = 1,10,000 / 11,000 = Rs.10. Because the money in and the units created are both priced at NAV, they offset exactly and the per-unit value is unchanged. NAV moves only when the underlying securities change in value.

questions.stem: In the same Rs.10-NAV scheme (net assets Rs.1,00,000; 10,000 units), suppose the fund wrongly allots the incoming 1,000 units at the face value of Rs.10 while the true NAV had risen. This distinguishes a fair from an unfair allotment because...

options.text: allotting at a price different from the true NAV shifts value between old and new investors, hurting some of them
allotting at face value always gives every investor a higher NAV
options.misconception: Believing face-value allotment mechanically raises NAV for all

options.text: the number of units outstanding is unaffected by any allotment
options.misconception: Thinking fresh allotments never change units outstanding

options.text: redemptions and purchases are the only events that can ever change NAV
options.misconception: Believing investor transactions, not security prices, drive NAV

questions.explanation: When units are issued (or redeemed) at a price that is not the true NAV, the money brought in no longer matches the value of the units created, so wealth is transferred between existing and new unit-holders and every investor is affected. A transaction done correctly at NAV, by contrast, leaves NAV untouched.

questions.stem: Anita holds 1,000 units bought at NAV Rs.10. The NAV later rises to Rs.12. What is the value of her holding now, and why did it change?

options.text: Rs.12,000, because the value of the portfolio's securities rose, lifting the NAV
Rs.10,000, because the value stays fixed until she redeems
options.misconception: Thinking a holding's value is frozen at the purchase price until sale

options.text: Rs.12,000, because other investors bought more units
options.misconception: Attributing the NAV rise to inflows rather than security prices

options.text: Rs.2,000, counting only the gain and dropping the original capital
options.misconception: Confusing the total value with the profit alone

questions.explanation: Holding value = units x current NAV = 1,000 x 12 = Rs.12,000. The NAV climbed from 10 to 12 because the securities the fund owns gained value, not because of any buying or selling of units. The value is marked to the current NAV every business day, not frozen at cost.

concepts.title: Open-Ended, Closed-Ended and Interval Fund Structures
concepts.description: A scheme's structure decides how and when an investor can put money in or take it out. Open-ended schemes accept fresh purchases and allow redemptions on any business day at NAV-based prices, so their pool of units keeps changing. Closed-ended schemes sell units only during the NFO for a fixed maturity; after that investors can exit only by selling on a stock exchange where the units are listed, so the number of units stays fixed. Interval funds are a hybrid: they are essentially closed-ended but turn open-ended during pre-announced transaction windows when investors can buy and redeem directly. Each such window must be at least two days long, and consecutive windows must be at least 15 days apart; like closed-ended funds they must be listed on an exchange.
prerequisites: Units, NAV and Why Transactions Don't Move the Price
misconceptions: Thinking a closed-ended scheme lets you redeem with the fund any day like an open-ended one
Believing interval funds are open every day
Assuming open-ended schemes have a fixed maturity date

objectives.text: Distinguish open-ended, closed-ended and interval schemes by how investors enter and exit.
State the SEBI timing rules that govern an interval fund's transaction windows.

questions.stem: Vikram wants a scheme he can add to or exit on any business day directly with the fund at NAV. Which structure fits?

options.text: An open-ended scheme
A closed-ended scheme
options.misconception: Thinking a closed-ended fund allows daily direct redemption with the fund

options.text: An interval fund
options.misconception: Overlooking that an interval fund is open only during pre-set windows

options.text: A New Fund Offer that never closes
options.misconception: Misreading the NFO as a permanent open subscription

questions.explanation: Only an open-ended scheme takes fresh money and pays out redemptions on any business day at NAV-based prices. A closed-ended scheme can be exited only by selling on the exchange after the NFO; an interval fund is open just during announced windows; and an NFO is a one-time launch period, not an ongoing structure.

questions.stem: After the NFO of a closed-ended scheme has ended, how does an investor exit before maturity?

options.text: By selling the units to another buyer on the stock exchange where they are listed
By redeeming directly with the fund at NAV on any business day
options.misconception: Applying open-ended redemption to a closed-ended scheme

options.text: By waiting for the next interval window to redeem
options.misconception: Confusing a closed-ended scheme with an interval fund

options.text: By surrendering units to the sponsor for a refund
options.misconception: Inventing a sponsor buy-back that does not exist

questions.explanation: Closed-ended schemes have a fixed unit count and no direct redemption after the NFO, so they must be listed and investors exit by trading the units on the exchange. Direct daily redemption belongs to open-ended schemes; interval windows belong to interval funds.

questions.stem: An interval fund announces its transaction windows. Which pair of timing rules is correct?

options.text: Each window is at least two days long, and consecutive windows are at least 15 days apart
Each window lasts at least 15 days, with a two-day gap between windows
options.misconception: Swapping the minimum window length with the minimum gap

options.text: Windows open every business day, like an open-ended fund
options.misconception: Treating interval funds as continuously open

options.text: Windows may be any length the AMC likes, with no minimum gap
options.misconception: Assuming SEBI sets no timing constraints on interval funds

questions.explanation: SEBI requires each transaction window to run for a minimum of two days, with a minimum gap of 15 days between two windows. The other options either swap the two numbers, or wrongly treat the fund as always open or entirely unregulated on timing.

concepts.title: Categories of Equity Funds
concepts.description: Equity funds invest mainly in company shares and differ by how they pick stocks. Passive/index funds simply copy an index, so no fund manager judgement selects securities; active funds try to beat the index by choosing stocks. Diversified equity funds spread across sectors and company sizes, lowering the damage if a few stocks do badly. By company size: large-cap funds buy big, stable, easily traded 'blue-chip' firms; mid-cap funds buy medium firms with faster growth but more vulnerability to downturns; small-cap funds buy the smallest firms for potentially higher gains and higher risk. Sector funds concentrate in one industry (higher risk, cyclical returns); theme funds span several sectors tied to one theme. Growth funds pick companies whose earnings should grow faster than average; value funds pick shares trading below their true worth; dividend-yield funds pick high-dividend payers. ELSS (Equity Linked Savings Scheme) is a tax-saving equity fund giving a Section 80C deduction up to Rs.1,50,000 a year, must hold at least 80% in equity, and locks money in for three years.
prerequisites: What a Mutual Fund Is and Who Runs It
misconceptions: Thinking an index fund manager actively picks winning stocks
Believing a sector fund is well diversified
Confusing ELSS's three-year lock-in with instant liquidity

objectives.text: Match an investor's need to the appropriate category of equity fund.
State the defining rules of an ELSS (lock-in, equity minimum, tax benefit).

questions.stem: How does an index fund differ from an active equity fund?

options.text: An index fund merely mirrors an index with no stock-selection judgement, while an active fund picks stocks to try to beat the index
An index fund's manager researches and hand-picks the best stocks to outperform the index
options.misconception: Reversing the roles: attributing active stock-picking to an index fund

options.text: An index fund guarantees a higher return than an active fund
options.misconception: Assuming passive management guarantees outperformance

options.text: An index fund holds only debt securities, unlike an active equity fund
options.misconception: Confusing the passive/active distinction with the equity/debt distinction

questions.explanation: An index (passive) fund simply replicates an index, so no manager decides which stocks to buy or when. An active fund selects securities on a strategy meant to beat the index. Neither guarantees a return, and an index equity fund still holds equity, not debt.

questions.stem: Sunil wants tax savings under Section 80C and is comfortable staying invested for a few years. Which equity fund suits him, and what is its lock-in?

options.text: An ELSS, with a three-year lock-in
A large-cap fund, with a one-year lock-in
options.misconception: Inventing a lock-in and 80C benefit for ordinary large-cap funds

options.text: A sector fund, with no lock-in but full 80C benefit
options.misconception: Attributing the 80C tax benefit to sector funds

options.text: An index fund, redeemable any day yet still 80C-eligible
options.misconception: Assuming index funds carry the ELSS tax deduction

questions.explanation: An Equity Linked Savings Scheme (ELSS) gives the Section 80C income-tax deduction (up to Rs.1,50,000 a year) and locks the money in for three years, during which it cannot be redeemed, transferred or pledged. Ordinary large-cap, sector or index funds carry no such 80C benefit or lock-in.

questions.stem: Priya wants to reduce the chance that the failure of a few stocks or one industry sinks her whole equity investment. Which fund type best meets this goal?

options.text: A diversified equity fund spread across sectors and company sizes
A sector fund concentrated in one industry
options.misconception: Believing a single-sector fund reduces concentration risk

options.text: A small-cap fund
options.misconception: Assuming small-cap concentration lowers rather than raises risk

options.text: A growth fund focused on the fastest-growing firms
options.misconception: Confusing a growth style with broad diversification

questions.explanation: A diversified equity fund holds stocks across many sectors and sizes, so poor performance in a few names or one sector does less damage. A sector fund is deliberately concentrated (higher risk), and small-cap or growth funds do not, by themselves, spread risk across the market.

questions.stem: A large-cap fund and a mid-cap fund are compared. Which statement is accurate?

options.text: Large-cap funds hold big, stable blue-chip firms; mid-cap funds hold medium firms with faster potential growth but more vulnerability in downturns
Mid-cap funds hold the largest, most liquid companies while large-cap funds hold medium ones
options.misconception: Swapping the definitions of large-cap and mid-cap

options.text: Both invest only in the top ten companies by size
options.misconception: Wrongly narrowing both categories to the same tiny set

options.text: Large-cap funds are riskier than mid-cap funds because they are bigger
options.misconception: Reversing the usual risk ranking between the two

questions.explanation: Large-cap funds buy large, liquid, blue-chip (well-established) companies with steady returns; mid-cap funds buy medium-sized companies that can grow faster but are more exposed to economic slowdowns, so they generally carry more risk than large-caps.

concepts.title: Debt Funds and Their Two Core Risks
concepts.description: Debt funds invest in instruments that pay a set income stream: government bonds, corporate bonds and money-market securities. Two risks dominate. Credit risk is the chance the borrower fails to pay interest or repay principal; a credit rating measures it, and a higher rating means lower default risk. Interest-rate risk is the chance bond prices move when market interest rates change; the longer a bond's tenor (time to maturity), the more its price swings when rates move. Fund types sit along these risks: liquid/money-market funds hold very short paper (under 91 days to maturity) and are lowest-risk; ultra-short-term (treasury/cash management) funds go up to 365 days; income funds hold a mix of short and long government and corporate debt and carry both interest-rate and credit risk; gilt funds hold only government securities so there is no default risk, but because they can be long-dated their prices are very sensitive to interest-rate changes.
prerequisites: Units, NAV and Why Transactions Don't Move the Price
misconceptions: Thinking gilt funds have no interest-rate risk because they carry no default risk
Believing a longer-tenor bond's price is less sensitive to rate changes
Assuming all debt funds are equally safe regardless of what they hold

objectives.text: Distinguish credit risk from interest-rate risk in a debt portfolio.
Rank debt fund categories by the risks they carry.

questions.stem: A gilt fund invests only in government securities. Which risk does it essentially avoid, and which does it still carry?

options.text: It avoids default (credit) risk but still carries interest-rate risk, especially if long-dated
It avoids interest-rate risk but still carries credit risk
options.misconception: Swapping which risk a gilt fund escapes

options.text: It avoids both credit and interest-rate risk entirely
options.misconception: Assuming government backing removes price risk too

options.text: It carries neither risk but has high default risk
options.misconception: Self-contradictory: denying and asserting default risk at once

questions.explanation: Government securities carry no default risk, so a gilt fund has essentially no credit risk. But their prices are very sensitive to interest-rate moves, and long-term gilt funds have higher interest-rate risk than short-term ones. So the interest-rate risk remains even though credit risk is gone.

questions.stem: Two bonds are identical except that Bond X matures in 1 year and Bond Y in 10 years. Market interest rates move sharply. What happens to their prices?

options.text: Bond Y's price moves much more than Bond X's, because a longer tenor means greater interest-rate sensitivity
Bond X's price moves more because shorter bonds are more sensitive
options.misconception: Reversing the tenor-sensitivity relationship

options.text: Both prices move by exactly the same amount, since the coupon is the same
options.misconception: Ignoring tenor's effect on price sensitivity

options.text: Neither price moves, because bond prices are fixed until maturity
options.misconception: Believing bond prices never respond to rate changes before maturity

questions.explanation: The longer the tenor (time to maturity), the greater a bond's price swing when interest rates change. So the 10-year Bond Y is far more sensitive than the 1-year Bond X. Bond prices do respond to rate changes in the market before maturity, and tenor, not just coupon, drives the size of the move.

questions.stem: A liquid (money-market) fund is described as the lowest-risk debt category. What feature of its holdings makes this so?

options.text: It holds very short-maturity debt securities (less than 91 days to maturity)
It holds only long-dated government bonds
options.misconception: Confusing liquid funds with long-dated gilt funds

options.text: It holds equity shares to cushion losses
options.misconception: Mistaking a debt fund for a hybrid holding equity

options.text: It is guaranteed against loss by SEBI
options.misconception: Assuming a regulatory guarantee that does not exist

questions.explanation: Liquid funds invest in debt maturing in under 91 days. Very short maturities mean small price swings when rates move and quick return of principal, which is why they are the lowest-risk debt category. They are not guaranteed, do not hold equity, and are the opposite of long-dated funds.

questions.stem: An income fund holds a mix of short- and long-term government and corporate debt. Which combination of risks does it face?

options.text: Both interest-rate risk and credit risk
Only credit risk, since government paper removes interest-rate risk
options.misconception: Assuming government paper cancels interest-rate risk in a mixed fund

options.text: Only interest-rate risk, since credit ratings remove default risk
options.misconception: Believing a rating eliminates rather than measures credit risk

options.text: Neither risk, because diversification cancels them out
options.misconception: Assuming a mixed debt portfolio is risk-free

questions.explanation: Because an income fund holds corporate debt (which can default) as well as long-dated paper (whose price moves with rates), it carries both credit risk and interest-rate risk. A credit rating only measures default risk; it does not remove it, and mixing does not make the portfolio risk-free.

concepts.title: Hybrid Funds, ETFs, Special Funds and How Mutual Funds Are Taxed
concepts.description: Some schemes go beyond a single asset class. Hybrid funds hold both equity and debt; a debt-oriented hybrid keeps 70-95% in conservatively managed debt with a small equity slice for a little extra return, is taxed as a debt fund, and a Monthly Income Plan is one example. Exchange Traded Funds (ETFs) trade on the exchange like a share, so their price is live and known in real time, unlike NAV which is struck once at end of day; a Gold ETF holds gold (each unit is about one gram of 99.5% purity). Arbitrage funds exploit price gaps between the cash and derivatives markets while staying fully hedged, giving low, liquid-fund-like volatility. International funds hold foreign securities; real-estate mutual funds hold property/related securities. On tax (2014 workbook rules): long-term capital gains (LTCG) from equity-oriented funds are nil and short-term gains (STCG) are taxed at 15%; for non-equity (debt) funds, gains are long-term only if units are held more than 36 months, LTCG is 20% with indexation (adjusting cost for inflation so only the real gain is taxed) and STCG is at the investor's marginal (own slab) rate.
prerequisites: Debt Funds and Their Two Core Risks
misconceptions: Thinking an ETF's price is struck only once a day like a normal fund's NAV
Believing debt-fund gains become long-term after 12 months like equity
Assuming indexation applies to equity-fund gains

objectives.text: Classify capital gains from equity vs non-equity funds by holding period and tax rate.
Explain how an ETF's real-time price differs from an ordinary scheme's end-of-day NAV.

questions.stem: Ravi redeems units of an equity-oriented fund 20 months after buying them, making a gain. Under the workbook's tax rules, how is this gain treated?

options.text: As long-term capital gain from an equity fund, which is exempt (nil tax)
As short-term capital gain taxed at 15%, because equity gains are always 15%
options.misconception: Ignoring the holding period and applying the STCG rate to a long-term equity gain

options.text: As long-term capital gain taxed at 20% with indexation
options.misconception: Applying the debt-fund LTCG rule to an equity fund

options.text: As tax-free only if held beyond 36 months
options.misconception: Applying the 36-month debt threshold to equity units

questions.explanation: For equity-oriented funds, units held more than 12 months give a long-term capital gain, which the workbook treats as nil (exempt). The 15% rate applies only to short-term equity gains, and the 20%-with-indexation and 36-month rules belong to non-equity (debt) funds, not equity.

questions.stem: Meera sells units of a debt fund 20 months after purchase. How is her gain classified and taxed under the workbook's rules?

options.text: As short-term capital gain, taxed at her marginal (slab) rate, because a debt gain is long-term only after 36 months
As long-term capital gain at 20% with indexation, since 20 months is more than a year
options.misconception: Applying the equity 12-month threshold to a debt fund

options.text: As tax-free, like long-term equity gains
options.misconception: Extending the equity LTCG exemption to debt funds

options.text: At a flat 15%, the short-term equity rate
options.misconception: Applying the equity STCG rate to a debt fund

questions.explanation: For non-equity (debt) funds, a gain is long-term only if units are held more than 36 months; 20 months is therefore short-term and taxed at the investor's marginal rate (their own income-tax slab). The 20%-with-indexation rate would apply only beyond 36 months, and the equity exemption/15% rate do not apply to debt funds.

questions.stem: What makes indexation valuable when computing long-term capital gains on a debt fund?

options.text: It raises the purchase cost for inflation, so only the real (inflation-adjusted) gain is taxed
It exempts the entire gain from tax
options.misconception: Confusing an inflation adjustment with a full exemption

options.text: It applies equally to long-term equity-fund gains
options.misconception: Extending indexation to equity gains, which are exempt anyway

options.text: It converts a short-term gain into a long-term one
options.misconception: Confusing a tax-computation step with the holding-period test

questions.explanation: Indexation adjusts the purchase price upward using the government's cost-inflation index, so the part of the gain that is merely inflation is not taxed and only the real gain is. It is not a full exemption, does not change the holding period, and is not used for equity funds.

questions.stem: How does the pricing of an ETF differ from an ordinary open-ended scheme?

options.text: An ETF trades on the exchange with a live, real-time price, whereas an ordinary scheme's NAV is struck once at end of day
An ETF's price is fixed for the whole day, while an ordinary scheme repriced every minute
options.misconception: Reversing which product has the real-time price

options.text: Both are priced only once a day at the same NAV
options.misconception: Ignoring the real-time trading feature of an ETF

options.text: An ETF has no price because it is not listed
options.misconception: Wrongly claiming ETFs are unlisted

questions.explanation: An ETF (Exchange Traded Fund) is bought and sold on the stock exchange like a share, so its price is known in real time and moves with the underlying index through the day. An ordinary open-ended scheme has one NAV computed at the end of each business day.

concepts.title: The Investing Process: PAN, KYC, Cut-off Timing and Plan Choice
concepts.description: Before investing, every category of investor needs a PAN (Permanent Account Number, the tax ID) and must be KYC-compliant (Know Your Customer identity verification), including an In-Person Verification (IPV) whose details a KYC Registration Agency (KRA) stores for reuse across intermediaries. Which NAV you get depends on the cut-off time. For a normal (non-liquid) purchase received at an official point of acceptance before 3.00 pm on a business day, you get that day's NAV; for a liquid-fund purchase the cut-off is 2.00 pm and, provided clear funds are in, you get the NAV of the day before. For any purchase of Rs.2 lakh or more, the applicable NAV is that of the day the fund actually has clear (usable) funds. Investors also choose a plan: a Direct Plan (no distributor) has a lower expense ratio, while a Regular Plan uses a distributor who earns commission, reflected in a higher expense ratio.
prerequisites: Units, NAV and Why Transactions Don't Move the Price
misconceptions: Thinking the cut-off time is the same for liquid and non-liquid funds
Believing a Regular Plan has a lower cost than a Direct Plan
Assuming the NAV depends only on submission time regardless of when funds clear for large investments

objectives.text: Determine the applicable NAV for a purchase given the fund type, time of receipt and amount.
Compare Direct and Regular plans on cost and use of a distributor.

questions.stem: Amit submits a purchase in a non-liquid equity scheme at an official point of acceptance at 1.30 pm on a business day, for Rs.50,000. Which NAV applies?

options.text: That same day's NAV, since it was received before the 3.00 pm cut-off
The previous day's NAV, as with a liquid fund
options.misconception: Applying the liquid-fund prior-day rule to a non-liquid fund

options.text: The next day's NAV, because purchases always settle a day later
options.misconception: Inventing a mandatory next-day rule for ordinary purchases

options.text: The NAV of whichever day the units are eventually dispatched
options.misconception: Confusing unit dispatch with the NAV-determination date

questions.explanation: For a non-liquid purchase received before the 3.00 pm cut-off on a business day, and below Rs.2 lakh, the applicable NAV is that day's NAV. The prior-day rule is specific to liquid funds; there is no automatic next-day rule; and NAV is set by receipt/clear-funds timing, not dispatch.

questions.stem: Neha invests Rs.5 lakh in an equity scheme, well before the 3.00 pm cut-off, but her money reaches the fund as clear funds only the next business day. Which NAV applies?

options.text: The NAV of the day on which clear funds are actually available to the fund
That day's NAV, because she submitted before 3.00 pm
options.misconception: Ignoring the special Rs.2-lakh-and-above clear-funds rule

options.text: The previous day's NAV, as for a liquid fund
options.misconception: Applying the liquid-fund rule to a large equity purchase

options.text: The lowest NAV of the two days, to protect the investor
options.misconception: Inventing an investor-favourable rule that does not exist

questions.explanation: For any investment of Rs.2 lakh and above, the applicable NAV is that of the day the fund receives clear (usable) funds, regardless of submission time. So Neha gets the next day's NAV. The before-cut-off rule and the liquid-fund prior-day rule do not override the large-investment clear-funds condition.

questions.stem: Compared with a Direct Plan, a Regular Plan of the same scheme has...

options.text: a higher expense ratio, because the distributor is paid a commission
a lower expense ratio, because it skips the distributor
options.misconception: Reversing which plan is cheaper

options.text: no expense ratio at all, since the AMC absorbs all costs
options.misconception: Assuming a plan can carry zero expenses

options.text: a different NAV rule that ignores cut-off times
options.misconception: Inventing a separate NAV mechanism for regular plans

questions.explanation: A Regular Plan uses a distributor who earns a commission paid by the fund, which shows up as a higher expense ratio (the annual cost charged to the scheme). A Direct Plan skips the distributor, so it has the lower expense ratio. Cut-off rules are the same for both.

concepts.title: Systematic Facilities: SIP, STP, SWP, Switch and Rupee Cost Averaging
concepts.description: Mutual funds offer facilities to automate investing. A Systematic Investment Plan (SIP) invests a fixed sum at regular intervals; because the same rupee amount buys more units when the NAV is low and fewer when it is high, the average cost per unit is pulled below the simple average of the NAVs. This benefit is called rupee cost averaging, and it works without any market timing. A Systematic Transfer Plan (STP) moves money in instalments from one scheme (source) to another (target) within the same folio, useful to shift gradually from, say, equity to short-term debt as a goal nears. A Systematic Withdrawal Plan (SWP) redeems a fixed amount at intervals to give regular cash flow. A Switch is a single, one-time move of the whole amount from one scheme/option to another. STP and switch redemptions attract exit loads and taxes as applicable.
prerequisites: Units, NAV and Why Transactions Don't Move the Price
misconceptions: Thinking rupee cost averaging requires timing the market
Confusing an STP (instalments) with a one-time switch
Believing the average cost per unit equals the simple average of the NAVs

objectives.text: Compute the average cost per unit under a SIP and compare it with the simple average NAV.
Select the correct systematic facility (SIP/STP/SWP/switch) for a stated need.

questions.stem: Deepa runs a SIP of Rs.3,000 a month for three months at NAVs of Rs.15, Rs.12 and Rs.10. What is her average cost per unit, and how does it compare with the simple average of the three NAVs (Rs.12.33)?

options.text: Rs.12.00 per unit, which is below the simple average of Rs.12.33
Rs.12.33 per unit, exactly equal to the simple average of the NAVs
options.misconception: Assuming average cost equals the simple average NAV

options.text: Rs.13.00 per unit, above the simple average of the NAVs
options.misconception: Believing SIP raises the average cost above the mean NAV

options.text: Rs.9,000 per unit, using total money invested as the per-unit cost
options.misconception: Confusing total invested with cost per unit

questions.explanation: Units each month = amount / NAV: 3000/15 = 200; 3000/12 = 250; 3000/10 = 300; total = 750 units for Rs.9,000 invested. Average cost = 9,000 / 750 = Rs.12.00. That is below the simple average NAV of (15+12+10)/3 = Rs.12.33, because the fixed sum buys more units when the NAV is low. This is rupee cost averaging.

questions.stem: Which statement about rupee cost averaging is correct?

options.text: It lowers the average purchase cost simply by investing a fixed sum regularly, with no need to time the market
It works only if the investor buys more when prices are high
options.misconception: Reversing the mechanism of cost averaging

options.text: It guarantees a profit regardless of how the market moves
options.misconception: Overstating cost averaging as a profit guarantee

options.text: It requires predicting market tops and bottoms to succeed
options.misconception: Believing cost averaging depends on market timing

questions.explanation: A fixed rupee amount automatically buys more units when the NAV is low and fewer when it is high, pulling the average cost down, with no forecasting needed. It does not require buying more at high prices, does not guarantee profit, and specifically avoids the need to time the market.

questions.stem: As his son's college fees approach, Ganesh wants to shift his equity-fund corpus gradually into a short-term debt fund over several months rather than in one lump. Which facility fits, and why not a single redemption?

options.text: A Systematic Transfer Plan (STP), because moving all at once risks doing so at a low NAV
A single Switch, because gradual transfer is not allowed between schemes
options.misconception: Denying that instalment transfers between schemes exist

options.text: A Systematic Withdrawal Plan (SWP) into his equity fund
options.misconception: Confusing SWP with transferring between two schemes

options.text: A fresh SIP into the equity fund
options.misconception: Choosing an investing plan when the need is to move out gradually

questions.explanation: An STP moves the corpus in instalments from the source (equity) to the target (short-term debt) fund, averaging out the NAVs and avoiding the risk that a single redemption lands on a low-NAV day. A switch is a one-time move; an SWP is for periodic cash withdrawals; and a fresh SIP would add to equity, not reduce it.

questions.stem: How does a Switch differ from an STP?

options.text: A switch is a single one-time transfer of the amount from one scheme/option to another, while an STP does it in instalments over time
A switch spreads the transfer over many instalments, while an STP is one-time
options.misconception: Swapping the definitions of switch and STP

options.text: A switch avoids all exit loads and taxes, unlike an STP
options.misconception: Assuming a switch is free of loads and taxes

options.text: A switch can only move money into a bank account, not another scheme
options.misconception: Confusing a switch with a redemption to bank / SWP

questions.explanation: A switch is a single transfer of the whole amount from one scheme or option to another; an STP performs the transfer in periodic instalments. Both may attract exit loads and taxes as applicable, and a switch moves money between schemes, not to a bank account.

caselets.scenario: Lakshmi, a 34-year-old schoolteacher in Pune, has never invested in markets before and is nervous about picking shares herself. A friend suggests mutual funds. Lakshmi decides to start a Systematic Investment Plan of Rs.4,000 a month in a diversified equity scheme, choosing the Direct Plan to keep costs down. She also wants a small emergency corpus she can access on any business day, and is separately keen to save income tax under Section 80C this year. Before she can invest, the distributor tells her she must first obtain a PAN and complete the KYC formalities, including an in-person verification. Lakshmi wonders how a fixed monthly amount can possibly help her when share prices keep bouncing around, and whether the emergency money should go into the same equity scheme.
concept_titles: What a Mutual Fund Is and Who Runs It
The Investing Process: PAN, KYC, Cut-off Timing and Plan Choice
Systematic Facilities: SIP, STP, SWP, Switch and Rupee Cost Averaging
Debt Funds and Their Two Core Risks

questions.stem: Why does Lakshmi need a PAN and KYC completed before her first investment?

options.text: They are mandatory regulatory prerequisites for every category of mutual fund investor
Only investors above a certain age must complete them
options.misconception: Believing PAN/KYC apply only to some investors by age

options.text: They are needed only for redemptions, not purchases
options.misconception: Confusing entry requirements with exit formalities

options.text: They replace the need to choose a scheme
options.misconception: Confusing identity compliance with scheme selection

questions.explanation: A PAN (tax ID) and KYC compliance, including in-person verification, are required of all categories of investors before investing in a mutual fund. They are entry prerequisites, apply regardless of age, and are separate from choosing a scheme.

questions.stem: Lakshmi picks the Direct Plan over the Regular Plan of the same scheme. What is the direct consequence for her costs?

options.text: A lower expense ratio, because no distributor commission is built in
A higher expense ratio, because direct investors pay extra fees
options.misconception: Reversing which plan costs more

options.text: No difference, since expense ratios are identical across plans
options.misconception: Denying the direct/regular cost gap

options.text: A guaranteed higher return regardless of the market
options.misconception: Confusing a lower cost with a guaranteed return

questions.explanation: A Direct Plan carries no distributor commission, so its expense ratio (annual cost charged to the scheme) is lower than the Regular Plan's. Lower cost is not the same as a guaranteed return, and the two plans are not identically priced.

questions.stem: Given her worry about bouncing share prices, how should the SIP's fixed monthly amount actually help Lakshmi?

options.text: Through rupee cost averaging: Rs.4,000 buys more units when the NAV is low and fewer when it is high, lowering her average cost with no market timing
By locking in the highest NAV each month
options.misconception: Misreading cost averaging as buying at the highest price

options.text: By guaranteeing she never loses money in equity
options.misconception: Treating SIP as a capital guarantee

options.text: By requiring her to predict market movements each month
options.misconception: Believing SIP depends on forecasting the market

questions.explanation: A fixed rupee amount automatically buys more units at low NAVs and fewer at high NAVs, so her average cost per unit is pulled down over time, without any need to time the market. It does not guarantee against loss or require forecasting.

questions.stem: Lakshmi wants a separate emergency corpus she can access on any business day. Combining what she needs (daily access and low risk) with fund knowledge, which choice fits best, and why not the equity scheme?

options.text: A liquid fund, because it holds very short-maturity debt (under 91 days) and allows any-business-day access, unlike volatile equity
The same diversified equity scheme, since equity is always liquid and safe
options.misconception: Assuming equity is low-risk and ideal for emergencies

options.text: A closed-ended scheme, because it can be exited any day
options.misconception: Wrongly attributing daily exit to a closed-ended scheme

options.text: A long-term gilt fund, because government backing makes it emergency-proof
options.misconception: Ignoring the high interest-rate price risk of long gilt funds

questions.explanation: An emergency corpus needs low risk and ready access. A liquid fund holds sub-91-day debt with minimal price swings and open-ended daily access. Equity is volatile (unsuitable for emergencies), a closed-ended scheme cannot be redeemed daily with the fund, and a long-term gilt fund, though default-free, has high interest-rate price risk.

questions.stem: For the Section 80C tax saving she wants this year, which equity product should Lakshmi use, and what must she accept?

options.text: An ELSS, accepting a three-year lock-in on the invested amount
Her ordinary diversified equity SIP, which itself gives an 80C deduction
options.misconception: Assuming ordinary equity funds carry the 80C benefit

options.text: A liquid fund, which is 80C-eligible and fully liquid
options.misconception: Attributing the 80C benefit to liquid funds

options.text: A gilt fund, since government securities qualify for 80C
options.misconception: Assuming government-security funds give an 80C deduction

questions.explanation: The Section 80C deduction from a mutual fund comes specifically from an ELSS (Equity Linked Savings Scheme), which locks the money in for three years. Ordinary diversified equity, liquid and gilt funds do not carry the 80C benefit.

caselets.scenario: Rohit, a software engineer in Bengaluru, runs a SIP of Rs.5,000 a month in an equity-oriented fund. Over three consecutive months the scheme's NAV is recorded as Rs.20, Rs.25 and Rs.10. Rohit is comparing his experience with that of his uncle Prakash, who invested a lump sum in a debt fund two years ago and is now deciding whether to redeem. Rohit believes that because he has invested across three different NAVs, his average cost must simply equal the average of the three NAV figures. He also assumes that whether he sells his equity units after ten months or after fifteen months, the tax treatment will be identical. Prakash, meanwhile, thinks his two-year-old debt-fund gain will be taxed as a long-term gain just like his friend's equity fund. The family wants the numbers worked out precisely before anyone redeems.
concept_titles: Systematic Facilities: SIP, STP, SWP, Switch and Rupee Cost Averaging
Units, NAV and Why Transactions Don't Move the Price
Hybrid Funds, ETFs, Special Funds and How Mutual Funds Are Taxed

questions.stem: How many total units does Rohit's three months of Rs.5,000 SIP buy at NAVs of Rs.20, Rs.25 and Rs.10?

options.text: 850 units
750 units
options.misconception: Using an averaged NAV of Rs.20 for all three months instead of month-by-month division

options.text: 15,000 units
options.misconception: Treating total money invested as the unit count

options.text: 600 units
options.misconception: Dividing total investment by the highest NAV only

questions.explanation: Units bought each month = amount / that month's NAV: 5000/20 = 250; 5000/25 = 200; 5000/10 = 500. Total = 250 + 200 + 500 = 850 units. Dividing month-by-month (not by an averaged NAV) is essential.

questions.stem: What is Rohit's average cost per unit, and is his belief that it equals the simple average NAV (Rs.18.33) correct?

options.text: Rs.17.65 per unit (approx), which is below Rs.18.33, so his belief is wrong
Rs.18.33 per unit, so his belief is correct
options.misconception: Assuming average cost equals the simple average of the NAVs

options.text: Rs.20.00 per unit, the first month's NAV
options.misconception: Using the entry NAV as the average cost

options.text: Rs.15,000 per unit, the total invested
options.misconception: Confusing total money invested with per-unit cost

questions.explanation: Average cost = total invested / total units = 15,000 / 850 = Rs.17.65 (approx). The simple average NAV is (20+25+10)/3 = Rs.18.33. Because the fixed sum bought many more units at the low Rs.10 NAV, the average cost is pulled below the simple average, so Rohit's belief is wrong.

questions.stem: Rohit assumes selling his equity units after 10 months or 15 months gives the same tax. Combining the holding-period rule with the equity tax rate, what actually happens?

options.text: At 10 months it is a short-term gain taxed at 15%; at 15 months it is a long-term gain that is exempt, so the treatments differ
Both are long-term and exempt, so treatment is identical
options.misconception: Ignoring that under 12 months is short-term for equity

options.text: Both are short-term at 15%, so treatment is identical
options.misconception: Ignoring that over 12 months turns equity gains long-term/exempt

options.text: At 15 months it is taxed at 20% with indexation
options.misconception: Applying the debt-fund LTCG rule to equity units

questions.explanation: For equity-oriented funds, units held 12 months or less give a short-term gain taxed at 15%; held more than 12 months they give a long-term gain that is exempt. So 10 months (15% tax) and 15 months (nil tax) are treated differently. The 20%-with-indexation rule is for debt funds, not equity.

questions.stem: Prakash's debt-fund units have been held for 24 months. Contrasting the debt rule with the equity rule his friend enjoyed, how is his gain classified?

options.text: As a short-term gain, because a debt-fund gain is long-term only after more than 36 months; it is taxed at his marginal rate
As a long-term gain exempt from tax, like his friend's equity fund
options.misconception: Extending the equity exemption to a debt fund

options.text: As a long-term gain at 20% with indexation, since 24 months exceeds 12
options.misconception: Applying the equity 12-month threshold to a debt fund

options.text: As tax-free because he held it for more than a year
options.misconception: Assuming any one-year holding makes a debt gain tax-free

questions.explanation: For non-equity (debt) funds the long-term threshold is more than 36 months, so 24 months is short-term, taxed at Prakash's marginal (slab) rate. Unlike equity funds, debt-fund long-term gains are neither exempt nor triggered at 12 months.

questions.stem: If, on a day the scheme's NAV is Rs.10, another investor redeems units at that same NAV of Rs.10, what happens to the NAV for remaining unit-holders?

options.text: It stays at Rs.10, because the assets leaving are matched by the units cancelled
It falls, because redemptions always reduce the NAV
options.misconception: Believing outflows mechanically lower NAV even at NAV pricing

options.text: It rises, because fewer units now share the assets
options.misconception: Assuming fewer units automatically lifts NAV

options.text: It becomes Rs.0 for the redeeming investor's share
options.misconception: Confusing an individual's exit with a change in per-unit NAV

questions.explanation: When units are redeemed at the correct NAV, the drop in net assets is exactly matched by the fall in units outstanding, so the per-unit NAV is unchanged. Redemptions and purchases done at NAV never move the NAV; only changes in the value of the underlying securities do.
